lessons.title: Introduction to Welding Processes: MIG, TIG, Stick
lessons.body: Welding joins metal by melting it. In Africa, you'll mostly use three processes: Stick (SMAW), MIG (GMAW), and TIG (GTAW). Each has a different setup, cost, and use. Stick welding is the most common in rural workshops because it's cheap and works outdoors. You need a stick welder (like a 200-amp inverter), electrodes (e.g., E6013 for general work), a chipping hammer, and a wire brush. MIG welding uses a wire feeder and shielding gas (usually CO2 or Argon mix). It's faster and easier for beginners but needs a gas cylinder and regulator. TIG welding uses a tungsten electrode and a separate filler rod, giving precise, clean welds on thin metal or aluminium. It's slower and requires more skill. For sculpture, Stick is good for thick steel frames; MIG for quick fabrication; TIG for detailed or visible joints. Always wear a welding helmet (shade 10-13), leather gloves, and a leather apron. Work in a well-ventilated areaânever in a closed room. In many African cities, you can buy a 200-amp Stick welder for around $100-$200. MIG setups start at $300 with gas. TIG is most expensive. Start with Stick: it teaches you heat control and patience. Practice on scrap steel plates 3-5 mm thick. Set your amperage: 3.2 mm electrode at 90-120 amps. Strike an arc like a match, then maintain a tight arc. Listen to the soundâit should crackle like frying bacon. If it hums, your amps are too low. Keep a consistent travel speed. Clean your welds with a wire brush after each pass. Remember, welding is a skill built by repetition. Spend at least 30 minutes daily on scrap before you weld a sculpture.

lessons.title: MIG Welding: Setup and Basic Beads
lessons.body: MIG welding (Metal Inert Gas) is like a hot glue gun for metal. You pull the trigger, wire feeds out, and an arc melts it into the joint. It's the easiest process to learn for sculpture because you can use two hands. First, set up your machine: a MIG welder (e.g., 180-amp), a gas cylinder (75% Argon / 25% CO2 for steel), a regulator, and a wire spool (0.8 mm or 0.9 mm ER70S-6 wire). Connect the ground clamp to your workbench. Set voltage and wire speed. For 3 mm steel, start with voltage at 18-19V and wire speed at 4-5 (on a 1-10 dial). The gas flow should be 10-15 CFH. Too much gas wastes it; too little gives porous welds. Before welding, clean metal to bare shine with a grinder. Position your gun at a 10-15 degree push angle. Stick out the wire about 10 mm. Wear a auto-darkening helmet (shade 10-11). Practice on a flat plate: make straight beads. Keep a consistent travel speedâabout 3-5 mm per second. Listen for a steady sizzle. If it pops, increase wire speed or voltage. For a basic bead, move in a slight zigzag or straight drag. Don't weave too wideâkeep beads 6-8 mm wide. After each bead, let it cool, then chip slag if any (MIG has little slag). Clean with a wire brush. In Africa, MIG wire and gas are available in major cities like Nairobi, Lagos, and Johannesburg. A 5 kg spool of wire costs $15-$25. Gas refill is $30-$50. Practice making 10 beads a day. Once you can run a straight bead without burn-through, try butt joints on 3 mm plates. That's your foundation for sculpture.

lessons.title: TIG Welding: Setup and Basic Beads
lessons.body: TIG welding (Tungsten Inert Gas) gives you the most control and the cleanest welds. It's perfect for visible joints on sculptures, thin sheet metal, and aluminium. But it's slower and needs two hands: one for the torch, one for the filler rod. Setup: a TIG welder (AC/DC for aluminium, DC for steel), a tungsten electrode (2% thoriated for steel, pure tungsten for aluminium), a gas lens, and 100% Argon gas. For steel, use DCEN (electrode negative). Grind the tungsten to a sharp point. Set amperage: for 1.6 mm steel, use 60-80 amps. Gas flow: 15-20 CFH. Use a foot pedal if you have one to control heat. Wear a TIG glove (thin leather) and a helmet with shade 10-12. Start by making a puddle on a scrap plate without filler. Hold the torch at a 70-degree angle, close to the metal (2-3 mm arc length). Once you have a shiny puddle, dip the filler rod (1.6 mm ER70S-2 for steel) into the front edge of the puddle. Move forward, dip, move, dip. Keep a rhythm. For a basic bead, travel speed should be slow and steadyâabout 2-3 mm per second. The weld should look like stacked dimes. If the puddle gets too big, reduce amps or move faster. For aluminium, use AC and a green tungsten. Clean aluminium with a stainless brush before welding. TIG is less common in rural Africa due to cost, but many technical colleges in cities like Accra and Durban teach it. A basic TIG welder costs $500-$800. Argon gas is $50-$80 per refill. Practice on 2 mm steel plates. Make 10 beads a day. Once you can control the puddle, try lap joints. TIG will make your sculptures stand out.

lessons.title: Brazing and Soldering Techniques
lessons.body: Brazing and soldering join metal without melting the base metal. They use a filler metal with a lower melting point. Soldering uses filler below 450Â°C (lead-free solder for electronics, or silver solder for jewellery). Brazing uses filler above 450Â°C (like brass or bronze rods). For sculpture, brazing is great for joining copper, brass, and steel without warping thin sheets. You need a torch (propane or oxy-acetylene), flux, and filler rods. For brazing steel, use a bronze rod (e.g., silicon bronze) and white flux. Clean the metal to bare shine. Apply flux to the joint. Heat the joint evenly with a neutral flame (blue cone). When the flux bubbles and turns clear, touch the rod to the joint. It should melt and flow like honey. Don't heat the rod directlyâheat the metal. Capillary action pulls the filler into the joint. For a strong joint, keep the gap between parts at 0.05-0.1 mm. After brazing, clean off flux with hot water and a wire brush. Soldering is for small, delicate work. Use a soldering iron (30-60W) or a small torch. For copper sculptures, use silver solder (hard solder) with borax flux. Heat the joint, apply solder, and let it flow. In Africa, brazing rods and flux are available at hardware stores in cities. A propane torch kit costs $30-$50. Oxy-acetylene is more expensive ($200+). Practice on scrap copper pipes. Make lap joints and T-joints. Brazing is ideal for repairing cast iron or joining dissimilar metals. It's also safer than welding for thin materials. Remember: ventilation is criticalâflux fumes are toxic. Work outdoors or use a fan. With practice, you can create seamless joints that look like solid metal.

lessons.title: Mechanical Fastening: Bolts, Rivets, and Screws
lessons.body: Not every joint needs welding. Mechanical fastening is strong, removable, and doesn't require heat. For sculpture, it lets you assemble and disassemble, or combine materials like wood and metal. Bolts: use grade 8.8 or stainless steel. For 6 mm bolts, drill a 6.5 mm hole. Tighten with a spanner or socket set. Add washers to spread load. For a permanent but low-profile joint, use rivets. Pop rivets (blind rivets) are easy: drill a hole, insert rivet, squeeze with a rivet gun. They work on thin sheets (up to 6 mm total thickness). For stronger joints, use solid rivetsâheat them, insert, and hammer the tail. Screws: self-tapping screws cut their own threads in pilot holes. For metal, use machine screws with nuts. In Africa, bolts and rivets are sold in most hardware stores. A box of 100 pop rivets (4 mm) costs $5-$10. A rivet gun is $15-$25. For sculpture, consider using bolts as design featuresâleave them exposed. Use lock nuts (nylon insert) to prevent loosening. When joining dissimilar metals (e.g., steel and aluminium), use nylon washers to prevent galvanic corrosion. Always drill pilot holes slightly smaller than the screw for self-tapping. For rivets, the hole should match the rivet diameter. Practice on scrap: make a lap joint with bolts, then with rivets. Test the strength by pulling apart. Mechanical fastening is reversible, so it's great for prototypes. In rural areas where welding gas is scarce, fastening is a reliable alternative. Keep a set of drill bits (3 mm to 10 mm), a hand drill or drill press, and a good rivet gun. Your sculpture can be a mix of welded and bolted parts for both strength and visual interest.

lessons.title: Project: Welded Geometric Sculpture
lessons.body: Now you'll build a welded geometric sculpture using the skills from this module. Choose a simple design: a cube frame, a pyramid, or an abstract star. For a cube, you need 12 pieces of 10 mm square steel bar, each 30 cm long. Cut them with an angle grinder or hacksaw. Clean ends with a grinder. Set up a jig: use a flat steel table or a thick wooden board with nails to hold pieces at 90 degrees. Tack weld each corner firstâsmall 5 mm welds on opposite sides to prevent distortion. Use your Stick or MIG welder. For 10 mm steel, set Stick amps to 110-130 with a 3.2 mm electrode, or MIG at 19-20V and wire speed 5. Check squareness with a carpenter's square. After tacking all corners, weld full joints. Alternate sides to balance heat. Let it cool, then grind welds smooth if desired. For a pyramid, use 4 pieces for base, 4 for sides, and 1 for top. Tack and weld. For an abstract star, cut 5 pieces of 8 mm round bar, each 40 cm, and weld them at the center. Use a metal pipe as a central hub. After welding, clean with a wire brush and apply a rust-preventive primer. If you want a finish, use black spray paint or clear lacquer. This project takes 4-6 hours. Work in a ventilated area. Wear all safety gear. In Africa, you can source steel bars from local scrap yards or hardware stores. A 6 m length of 10 mm square bar costs $8-$12. This sculpture can be a small table piece or a garden ornament. Once you master the cube, try more complex polyhedra. The key is to measure twice, cut once, and tack before full welding. Show your finished piece to your instructor or post it online for feedback. Congratulationsâyou're now a metal sculptor.

quiz.q: Which welding process is most common in rural African workshops due to low cost and outdoor capability?
quiz.explanation: Stick welding is cheap, portable, and works outdoors, making it ideal for rural areas.

quiz.q: What is the recommended amperage for a 3.2 mm stick electrode on mild steel?
quiz.explanation: A 3.2 mm electrode typically runs at 90-120 amps for general welding.

quiz.q: Which shielding gas is commonly used for MIG welding of steel?
quiz.explanation: A mix of 75% Argon and 25% CO2 provides good arc stability and penetration for steel.

quiz.q: What is the correct gas flow rate for MIG welding?
quiz.explanation: 10-15 CFH is standard for MIG to avoid porosity and waste.

quiz.q: In TIG welding, what type of tungsten electrode is used for steel?
quiz.explanation: 2% thoriated tungsten is common for DC TIG welding on steel.

quiz.q: What is the recommended amperage for TIG welding 1.6 mm steel?
quiz.explanation: 60-80 amps is typical for thin steel to avoid burn-through.

quiz.q: Which process uses a filler metal that melts below 450Â°C?
quiz.explanation: Soldering uses filler metals with melting points below 450Â°C.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of flux in brazing?
options: B) To clean and prevent oxidation
quiz.explanation: Flux cleans the metal and prevents oxide formation during brazing.

quiz.q: Which type of rivet is easiest for a beginner to use?
quiz.explanation: Pop rivets require only a drill and rivet gun, no hammering or heating.

quiz.q: What is the recommended hole size for a 6 mm bolt?
quiz.explanation: A 6.5 mm hole gives clearance for a 6 mm bolt.

quiz.q: Which welding process is best for thin sheet metal and visible joints?
quiz.explanation: TIG offers precise heat control and clean welds on thin materials.

quiz.q: What is the correct push angle for MIG welding?
quiz.explanation: A 10-15 degree push angle helps with visibility and penetration.

quiz.q: What should you listen for when Stick welding with correct settings?
options: B) A crackling sound like frying bacon
quiz.explanation: A crackling sound indicates proper arc stability and amperage.

quiz.q: Which gas is used for TIG welding?
quiz.explanation: Argon is the standard shielding gas for TIG welding.

quiz.q: What is the advantage of mechanical fastening over welding?
quiz.explanation: Mechanical fasteners can be disassembled and don't require heat.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a jig in a welded sculpture project?
options: A) To hold pieces at correct angles
quiz.explanation: A jig holds parts in place during tacking and welding.

quiz.q: What is the recommended shade for a welding helmet when Stick welding?
quiz.explanation: Shade 10-13 protects eyes from the bright arc of Stick welding.

quiz.q: Which filler rod is used for TIG welding steel?
quiz.explanation: ER70S-2 is a common mild steel TIG filler rod.

quiz.q: What is the correct gap for brazing joints?
quiz.explanation: A tight gap allows capillary action to pull filler into the joint.

quiz.q: What safety gear is essential for all welding processes?
quiz.explanation: A welding helmet, leather gloves, and apron protect from sparks and UV radiation.

quiz.q: What is the typical cost of a 200-amp Stick welder in Africa?
quiz.explanation: A basic 200-amp inverter Stick welder costs around $100-$200.

quiz.q: Which process is best for joining copper and brass without warping?
quiz.explanation: Brazing uses lower heat and is ideal for thin copper and brass.

quiz.q: What is the recommended wire diameter for MIG welding 3 mm steel?
quiz.explanation: 0.8 mm wire is suitable for 3 mm steel at typical voltages.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a lock nut?
options: A) To prevent loosening from vibration
quiz.explanation: Lock nuts have a nylon insert that grips the bolt to prevent loosening.

quiz.q: How many pieces of 10 mm square bar are needed for a cube frame?
quiz.explanation: A cube has 12 edges, so 12 pieces are needed.

quiz.q: What is the first step after cutting metal for a welded sculpture?
options: B) Clean ends with a grinder
quiz.explanation: Cleaning ends removes burrs and ensures good weld penetration.

quiz.q: What is the recommended gas flow for TIG welding?
quiz.explanation: 15-20 CFH provides adequate shielding for TIG welding.

quiz.q: Which type of flame is used for brazing?
quiz.explanation: A neutral flame (blue cone) is best for brazing to avoid oxidation.

quiz.q: What is the main risk of welding in a closed room?
options: B) Toxic fumes and lack of oxygen
quiz.explanation: Welding fumes are toxic and can displace oxygen in enclosed spaces.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of tack welding before full welding?
options: A) To hold parts in alignment
quiz.explanation: Tack welds temporarily hold parts in place to prevent distortion during full welding.
